# Merge Sort

## Summary

Sort an array ascending by splitting it in half, sorting each half recursively,
and merging the two sorted halves back together in linear time.

## Constraints

- Values may repeat and may be negative.
- The array may be empty.
- The sort must be stable: equal elements keep their original relative order
  (not observable with plain integers, but it is a property of the algorithm and
  the reason it is used on records).

## Examples

| Input | Output | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `[5, 2, 4, 1, 3, 6]` | `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` | |
| `[4, 3, 2, 1]` | `[1, 2, 3, 4]` | reverse order costs the same as any other |
| `[3, -1, 0, -7, 2]` | `[-7, -1, 0, 2, 3]` | |
| `[2, 1, 2, 1]` | `[1, 1, 2, 2]` | duplicates keep their relative order |

## Edge Cases

- Empty array and single element — both are already sorted, and both are the
  recursion's base case.
- Two elements, the smallest case where the merge actually chooses.
- All elements equal, where `<=` versus `<` in the merge decides stability.
- Odd lengths, where the two halves differ in size.
- Already-sorted and reverse-sorted input — merge sort does the same amount of
  work either way, unlike quicksort or insertion sort.

## Complexity

- **Time:** `O(n log n)` in the best, average and worst case — `log n` levels of
  recursion, each doing `O(n)` merging work.
- **Space:** `O(n)` for the merge buffers, plus `O(log n)` recursion stack. This
  is the price for the guaranteed worst case; quicksort is `O(log n)` space but
  `O(n²)` in the worst case.

## Why This Category

Merge sort is the clean example of divide and conquer: split into independent
subproblems, solve them recursively, then spend linear time combining. The merge
step itself — two pointers walking two sorted runs — is reusable on its own, for
merging k sorted lists, counting inversions, or external sorting of data too big
for memory.

## Thought Process

- The recursion is the easy half; the merge is where the bugs are. Remember to
  drain whichever run still has elements after the main loop.
- `left[i] <= right[j]` (not `<`) is what makes the sort stable — taking from
  the left run on a tie preserves the original order.
- The starter allocates new lists at each level, which is the readable version.
  The in-place variant with a single shared scratch buffer is the one to write
  when the allocation cost matters.
- Because the split is by position rather than value, the recursion tree is
  always balanced — that is exactly why the worst case cannot degrade.
